name: Negative-ion jewelry and wristbands

lead: Negative-ion jewelry and wristbands are worn pendants, bracelets and similar items sold online as emitting negative ions, scalar energy or quantum energy. Advertised benefits include reduced inflammation, better circulation, improved focus and anti-aging, and vendors credit minerals such as monazite sand, zeolite, germanium or tourmaline.

For appearance, the relevant claim is anti-aging and general vitality. Regulators have not assessed whether the products work as advertised, and analyses of some items found uranium and thorium. The US NRC and German BfS say whole-body dose is likely low, while advising against needless exposure.

paras: They are worn continuously on the wrist or neck, often under the label of balance or wellness, and are sold online as bands, watches, pendants, pillows and similar items. Items with a magnet or hologram are described by the NRC as probably not radioactive.

The NRC reports that an analysis of wrist bands and pendants found uranium and thorium above the level that requires a license, and notes continuous wear can raise skin dose from beta radiation. The Dutch institute estimated some skin doses above its local limit. Inhaling particles is a greater concern for pillows and mattresses.

angle.text: Sellers present the items as passive wellness accessories whose claimed effects include anti-aging. Regulators report that they have not evaluated those claims and have found radioactive material in some products.

lead: Negative-ion jewelry and wristbands are wearable products, including pendants and bands, sold online as emitting negative ions, scalar energy or quantum energy. Advertised benefits include reduced inflammation, better circulation, improved focus and anti-aging [1].

For people interested in looks, the anti-aging and wellness claims are the draw: sellers present the items as a passive way to support vitality while worn. Vendors often credit minerals such as monazite sand, zeolite, germanium or tourmaline [1].

Regulators have examined these products mainly for radioactivity. The US Nuclear Regulatory Commission and Germany's Federal Office for Radiation Protection report that some contain natural uranium and thorium, and both say they cannot confirm or find any scientific basis for the health claims [1][2].

paras: The NRC lists wrist bands, pendants, kinesiology tape, feminine products, pillows, mattresses and yoga pads among items sold online as emitting negative ions, scalar energy or quantum energy [1]. Germany's BfS describes terms such as negative ion energy and quantum scalar energy as marketing language without a scientific basis [2].

The NRC states that many of these products contain uranium-238, thorium-232 or radium-226, that an NRC-commissioned analysis of wrist bands and pendants found uranium and thorium above 0.05 percent by weight, enough to require a radioactive material license, and that some products contain none [1]. It states they have not been licensed by the NRC or any state and that it cannot say whether they work as advertised [1].

NRC and other agencies assess the whole-body dose from wearing a pendant or wristband as likely low, while continuous wear can raise skin dose from beta radiation and the Dutch institute found some skin doses exceeding its local limit. The NRC's advice for those who continue to use them is to limit contact time, increase distance and wear pendants over clothing [1].

The BfS analysed a pendant containing traces of thorium-series radionuclides and a small amount of uranium-238, suspected to come from minerals such as monazite sand. Its surface dose rate was about 160 nanosieverts per hour, and it saw no immediate, significant health risk but said exposure without benefit is unjustified, noting there is no scientific evidence of health benefits [2].
